narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 64.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking after the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted, signaling that your later academic performance raised serious concerns about readiness for the bar.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in the opposite direction. At 35, it is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, so it provided a modest pull toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the other signals.

Your family income bracket (middle) ranked third and added a smaller additional push toward failure. While many accepted students also come from middle-income families, this detail still contributed slightly to the model’s overall assessment.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic trajectory, especially the low third-year ranking, made success on the bar exam uncertain enough to deny admission at this time.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record and bar readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking targeted tutoring for the bar, or gaining practical legal experience that demonstrates your ability to improve. Once you can show clearer progress, reapply. Many students successfully follow this path.
